page_contents_html:
Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)

IBS is a common, chronic disorder of gut-brain interaction affecting approximately 10–20% of adults in the UK. It is more common in women (F:M ~2:1) and typically presents before the age of 50.

IBS is a positive clinical diagnosis based on symptom criteria — not simply a diagnosis of exclusion. It does not increase cancer risk and does not progress to inflammatory bowel disease.

Subtypes

  • IBS-C — predominant constipation
  • IBS-D — predominant diarrhoea
  • IBS-M — mixed bowel habit
  • IBS-U — unclassified (does not fit C, D, or M criteria)

Subtypes may change over time in the same patient. Symptom severity fluctuates and is often worsened by stress, diet, and intercurrent illness.

IBS has significant quality of life impact — patients report impaired work, social functioning, and psychological wellbeing. Co-existing anxiety and depression are common and should be addressed.

This pathway covers diagnosis and management for adults aged 16 and over in NHS Dumfries & Galloway primary care.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
Rome IV diagnostic criteria

IBS can be diagnosed when all of the following are met:

  • Recurrent abdominal pain, on average ≥1 day per week in the last 3 months
  • Associated with ≥2 of the following:
    • Related to defecation (pain improves or worsens)
    • Associated with a change in stool frequency
    • Associated with a change in stool form (appearance)
  • Symptom onset ≥6 months before diagnosis

Additional supportive symptoms (not required for diagnosis): bloating, mucus in stool, urgency, incomplete evacuation, straining.

Alarm features — must be excluded before diagnosing IBS

Presence of any alarm feature requires urgent assessment and should prompt alternative diagnosis/referral rather than IBS management:

  • Age >45 with new or changed bowel symptoms
  • Rectal bleeding (unexplained)
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Nocturnal symptoms waking patient from sleep
  • Family history of colorectal or ovarian cancer (first-degree)
  • Palpable rectal or abdominal mass
  • Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia
  • Inflammatory markers suggesting IBD

Investigations

For patients aged 16–45 with symptoms meeting Rome IV criteria and no alarm features, perform the following:

Blood tests:

  • FBC
  • U&Es
  • LFTs
  • TFTs
  • CRP (or ESR/plasma viscosity)
  • Ferritin
  • Anti-TTG (coeliac screen)

Stool tests:

  • Faecal calprotectin (all patients)
  • qFIT (if any concern re: colorectal cancer, or age >40)
  • MC&S and C. difficile toxin (if diarrhoea predominant)

Faecal calprotectin interpretation

  • <50 µg/g — Normal. Supports IBS diagnosis. Proceed to management.
  • 50–120 µg/g — Equivocal. Repeat after 4 weeks off NSAIDs (NSAIDs can cause false elevation). If still elevated, refer to gastroenterology.
  • >120 µg/g — Raised. Refer to gastroenterology to exclude IBD.

NSAID caution — false positive calprotectin

NSAIDs (including ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) can cause a false elevation in faecal calprotectin. If the result is equivocal (50–120 µg/g) and the patient is taking NSAIDs, stop NSAIDs where clinically safe and repeat the test after 4 weeks before referring.

Normal investigations

If bloods and faecal calprotectin are all normal and Rome IV criteria are met, a positive diagnosis of IBS can be made. No further routine investigation is required. Do not perform colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, barium enema, ultrasound, or hydrogen breath testing routinely.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
Management follows a stepped approach. Start with lifestyle and dietary advice for all patients. Escalate as needed based on symptom type and response.

Step 1 — Lifestyle and dietary advice (all patients, first line)

Provide at first presentation. Signpost to NHS Inform IBS and British Dietetic Association (BDA) resources.

  • Eat regular meals — do not skip meals
  • Drink ≥8 cups of fluid daily (water or non-caffeinated preferred)
  • Limit tea and coffee to ≤3 cups daily
  • Reduce alcohol and carbonated drinks
  • Limit fresh fruit to 3 portions per day
  • If constipation: avoid insoluble fibre (wheat bran); try soluble fibre (oats, linseeds)
  • If diarrhoea: avoid sorbitol-containing foods (sugar-free sweets, some diet drinks)
  • Probiotics: trial for ≥4 weeks at manufacturer-recommended dose — continue only if benefit is clear
  • Regular physical activity and stress reduction
  • Avoid aloe vera products for IBS

Step 2 — Refer to NHS D&G Dietetics

  • If symptoms persist despite general dietary advice
  • Dietitian can supervise exclusion diets and low FODMAP diet
  • Low FODMAP diet must only be undertaken under dietitian supervision — not to be started by patient independently

Step 3 — Drug therapy by symptom type

Choose drugs based on the predominant symptom. Drugs can be used in combination if multiple symptoms are present.

Bloating, wind, and/or abdominal pain

  • Peppermint oil — antispasmodic; take before meals (e.g. Colpermin 1 capsule three times daily before meals)
  • Mebeverine 135 mg three times daily, 20 minutes before meals ✓ First Choice
  • Hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) 10–20 mg up to four times daily as needed
  • Amitriptyline 5–10 mg nocte; titrate to effect (usually ≤30 mg); review at 4 weeks then 6–12 monthly — unlicensed indication; informed consent required
  • Nortriptyline 10–30 mg nocte (second TCA option if amitriptyline not tolerated) — unlicensed indication; informed consent required

Diarrhoea-predominant (IBS-D)

  • Loperamide 2 mg after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day); titrate to achieve Bristol Stool Form type 4 ✓ First Choice
  • Amitriptyline (as above) — also useful in IBS-D; reduces bowel frequency
  • Ondansetron 4 mg up to three times daily — for severe/refractory IBS-D where loperamide inadequate; verify local formulary position

Constipation-predominant (IBS-C)

  • Ispaghula husk (e.g. Fybogel) 1 sachet twice daily with water ✓ First Choice
  • Macrogol (e.g. Movicol) 1–3 sachets daily — if ispaghula insufficient; avoid lactulose
  • Linaclotide 290 micrograms once daily — only after laxatives have failed AND symptoms present ≥12 months; ✓ Specialist Initiation Only
  • Prucalopride 1–2 mg once daily — secondary care initiation only; ✓ Specialist Initiation Only

Step 4 — Psychological support

  • Consider referral for CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy, or psychological therapy if IBS remains refractory after 12 months of primary care management
  • Address co-existing anxiety or depression — this significantly affects IBS symptoms
  • In NHS D&G, refer via PCMHT or discuss local psychology/IAPT-equivalent access routes with patient

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Urgent / USOC — refer if any alarm feature present

  • Age >45 with new or changed bowel symptoms — refer via 2-week wait (suspected cancer pathway) or USOC as appropriate
  • Rectal bleeding — unexplained
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Palpable abdominal or rectal mass
  • Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia
  • Nocturnal symptoms waking patient from sleep
  • First-degree family history of colorectal or ovarian cancer with new bowel symptoms

Do not apply IBS management while alarm features are unresolved. Refer first.

Routine — refer to gastroenterology

  • Faecal calprotectin >120 µg/g — to exclude IBD
  • Faecal calprotectin 50–120 µg/g — equivocal and not settling after repeat (off NSAIDs)
  • Abnormal blood results suggesting alternative diagnosis (e.g. positive TTG, unexplained anaemia, markedly raised CRP)
  • Diagnostic uncertainty after full primary care assessment
  • Failure to respond to ≥12 months of adequate primary care management

Routine — refer to NHS D&G Dietetics

  • Symptoms persisting despite general dietary and lifestyle advice
  • To supervise low FODMAP or other elimination diet

Routine — psychological referral

  • Refractory IBS with significant psychological comorbidity (anxiety, depression, health anxiety)
  • Referral for CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy, or psychological therapy — via PCMHT or local psychology access in NHS D&G
  • Consider after 12 months of primary care management without adequate response

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
The following patients can be managed in primary care without specialist referral:

  • Confirmed IBS diagnosis with Rome IV criteria met, no alarm features, and normal investigations (bloods + faecal calprotectin <50 µg/g)
  • Patients whose symptoms are adequately controlled with lifestyle modifications, dietary changes, or first-line drug therapy
  • Patients who decline investigation or intervention beyond primary care
  • Patients with well-established, long-standing IBS with a previous specialist review and no change in symptoms
  • Young adults (16–45) with typical IBS-D or IBS-C, normal investigations, and no alarm features — reassure and manage in primary care

IBS does not increase risk of colorectal cancer or progression to IBD. Reassurance of this is an important part of the primary care consultation and helps reduce re-attendance.

Avoid routine colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, barium enema, ultrasound, or hydrogen breath testing in confirmed IBS without alarm features.

notes_for_editor: NICE CKS URL returned HTTP 403 — manual check of CKS IBS page recommended before publishing to confirm no material differences from CG61.

BSG 2021 full-text guidelines (Gut 70:1214) were behind paywall and not accessible. Recommendations on ondansetron, linaclotide, and prucalopride are based on QURIS pathway content and NICE CG61. Verify against BSG guidelines.
Ondansetron in IBS-D: not licensed for IBS — verify local NHS D&G formulary position and consider adding unlicensed note if required.
Amitriptyline and Nortriptyline: both unlicensed for IBS. Informed consent required per NICE CG61. Flagged in drug lists.
Linaclotide and Prucalopride: marked as Specialist Initiation Only per QURIS. NICE CG61 specifies linaclotide after laxative failure AND ≥12 months symptoms — reflected in pathway.
Psychology referral route: NHS D&G equivalent of IAPT — confirm current referral pathway (PCMHT vs. self-referral) with local mental health lead before publishing.
Low FODMAP diet note: per NICE CG61 and D&G context, must be supervised by dietitian. Included in dietetics referral section.
Rome IV criteria used (per QURIS) rather than NICE CG61 older criteria — this is the current international standard and appropriate.
qFIT reference in investigations: included per QURIS for patients >40 or where CRC concern exists. Not in NICE CG61 original (predates qFIT rollout) — clinically appropriate addition.
